analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators ban traders who manipulate electricity or natural gas markets from energy trading.
analysis.headline: A bill to let federal regulators ban energy market manipulators from trading has 13 House Democrats behind it and has sat untouched in committee since April 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill strengthens federal enforcement against energy market manipulation. It would let the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission bar, temporarily or permanently, anyone found to have manipulated electricity or natural gas markets — or filed false market information — from buying or selling energy or transmission services. It would also make it a violation to knowingly file false information with gas price-reporting agencies.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay electricity and natural gas bills, since manipulation of wholesale energy markets can inflate the prices that flow through to consumers. Honest energy market participants also benefit from competitors being barred for cheating. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and businesses paying energy bills

how_it_helps.text: Gives the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission power to prohibit or suspend, temporarily or permanently, any person who manipulates electricity markets from trading electric energy, energy products such as financial transmission rights, or transmission services.

Extends the same trading-ban authority to natural gas, covering anyone who violates the Natural Gas Act's manipulation or false-reporting rules, and creates a new prohibition on knowingly filing false information with federal or private gas price-reporting agencies.

Broadens existing civil penalty provisions from 'individuals' to any 'person', so firms themselves — not just employees — can face consequences for manipulation, and covers indirect as well as direct trading.

analysis.who_pays: Energy trading firms and power and gas marketers that could face temporary or permanent bans from energy markets if caught manipulating prices or filing false data. The enforcement itself costs taxpayers little since the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission already exists and would simply gain a new tool. [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy trading firms that manipulate markets

drawbacks.text: The bill is enforcement-only: it adds penalties for manipulation but does nothing to change market structure, cap prices, or directly lower bills, and its effect on consumer prices depends entirely on how vigorously regulators use the new authority.

The trading-ban language is broad — it covers trading 'directly or indirectly' and gives the Commission discretion over how long a ban lasts — which critics could argue risks sweeping in legitimate trading activity or being applied unevenly.
As a minority-party bill with only 12 cosponsors and no Senate companion visible in the record, its practical prospects of changing anyone's energy bill in this Congress are slim.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real but indirect: if manipulation inflates wholesale electricity and gas prices, a credible threat of being banned from trading could deter it, and the direct fiscal cost is minimal since it builds on an existing regulator's authority. The downside is that the bill is a narrow tool — it does not lower prices on its own, its breadth could invite disputes over legitimate trading, and its chances of enactment this Congress appear very low. On balance it is a modest, low-cost consumer protection, not a structural fix for high energy bills.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not acted on it, so it is still waiting with no hearing or vote so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on April 21, 2026, joined by 12 Democratic cosponsors including Reps. Beyer, Casten, Jayapal, Huffman, and Lofgren.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is where the record ends — no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.
The Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive but has seen no committee action in the months since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy trading firms are better off so far: a bill that could ban manipulators from electricity and gas markets has sat in committee without action, and consumers have gained nothing yet.

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand Federal Energy Regulatory Commission enforcement against energy market manipulation.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no recorded action on the bill since it was referred — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Brett Guthrie
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, controls whether the bill gets a markup or vote; none has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, so no partisan split can be measured; all 13 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support in the record.

industries.industry: Electricity and natural gas traders and marketers
industries.note: The bill's main target: firms or individuals found to have manipulated wholesale power or gas markets — or filed false data with price reporters — could be barred from buying or selling energy and transmission services. Manipulated wholesale prices flow into the bills ordinary households and businesses pay, so the industry's gain from light enforcement is the public's cost.

Utilities trading in wholesale markets face the new ban and penalty authority if they manipulate prices or report false data, but honest firms benefit from a cleaner market. Consumers ultimately pay utility rates, so enforcement against cheaters tends to work in their favor.

The bill makes it a violation to knowingly file false information with these agencies, raising the stakes on the data they compile. Their core business is untouched, but the accuracy of the price indexes they publish carries legal weight for the first time in this form.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced by minority-party members with a dozen cosponsors and no committee action in the months after referral rarely get a markup, let alone a floor vote, in a chamber run by the other party; unless the committee schedules action before the Congress ends in January 2027, the bill will die there and would need to be reintroduced.
